draft.title: Accuracy and usefulness of a source
card: A source is accurate when other evidence agrees with it. A historian checks it against other sources.
A source is useful when it helps answer the question being asked. The same source can be useful for one question and not for another.
A source can be accurate but not useful. A true list of a pharaoh's titles tells us little about how farmers lived.
A biased source favours one side. It can still be useful, because it shows what its writer wanted others to believe.
draft.remember: Accuracy asks if other evidence agrees. Usefulness asks if it helps with the question.

a.q: What makes a historian call a source accurate?
opts: Other evidence agrees with what it says
It answers the question the historian is asking
It was made by someone who lived at the time
It shows no sign of favouring any one side
a.why: A source is accurate when other evidence supports it. Answering the question is usefulness, which is a different test. Being made by someone at the time does not make a source accurate on its own.
a.clue: Think about checking one source against others.

b.q: A pharaoh's monument says he won a great battle, but other records suggest the battle was a draw. Maria asks how pharaohs wanted to be seen. Is the monument useful for her question?
opts: Yes, because it shows how the pharaoh wanted to be seen
No, because other records disagree with it
No, because a source that favours one side is never useful
Yes, but only if the monument is also accurate
b.why: Maria's question is about how the pharaoh wanted to be seen, and the monument shows that. Its bias lowers its accuracy about the battle, but it can still be useful. Usefulness depends on the question, not only on accuracy.
b.clue: Match the source to the question being asked.

a.best: Other evidence agrees with what it says

b.best: Yes, because it shows how the pharaoh wanted to be seen

problems.detail: Two distractors use absolute words ('never useful', 'only if accurate') where the card says a biased source 'can' still be useful. Students can rule them out by spotting the absolute word rather than by knowing the idea.
The right option repeats the question's own phrase ('how the pharaoh wanted to be seen'), so it stands out as matching the question without testing understanding of usefulness.
